narrative: The model estimates a 78% chance that you will leave your job, which is why the promotion decision was denied: the organization is treating the likely departure as a reason not to invest a promotion in you at this point. The strongest signal in this prediction is your total years of experience. You have 11 or more years overall, a level reached by only about 15% of employees the model expected to stay; in your case this extensive experience is read as increasing mobility and pushing the prediction toward leaving. The next most important signal is whether you have other job opportunities. You reported none, and most employees expected to stay also reported none; this factor works in the opposite direction, reducing the estimated chance of leaving and counting in your favor. The third signal is your time in the current organization. You have 1–5 years here; although this is common among employees predicted to stay, in your overall profile it still tilts the prediction toward leaving, perhaps reflecting a shorter current tenure alongside long total experience. Together, these signals outweigh the stabilizing effect of having no other opportunities, producing the 78% estimate. Before reconsidering promotion, the organization should discuss your career path, recognition, and retention plans with you, and you should clarify your intentions and what would make you stay. A retention conversation and a development plan would help test whether the departure risk is real and address it.
